title: The Blind Regulator: Ashby's Law and the Unavoidable Logic of Instructional Design
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick borrows W. Ross Ashby's cybernetic Law of Requisite Variety ("only variety can destroy variety") to argue that teaching is a regulatory enterprise: an instructional system can only control learner strategies it is able to detect. When teachers or assessments check only whether an answer is correct, the learner's repertoire of shortcuts (guessing from pictures, eliminating multiple-choice options, pattern-matching) passes through unregulated, so the appearance of learning is preserved while the intended cognitive operation never occurs. He uses this lens to explain why differentiation often failed, since it varied task difficulty rather than detecting strategy, and why pupils can perform well in class yet falter in exams. He then turns to adaptive platforms and AI tutors, which could in principle widen the diagnostic channel but mostly adapt only on difficulty and so leave strategy untouched. His prescription is to design tasks by asking how else a learner could succeed without the intended thinking, and to close those paths through worked solutions, varied formats and probing follow-ups. He concludes that requisite variety is an asymptote, so the honest response is continual observation and iteration rather than despair.
points: Binary correct/incorrect feedback is a low-capacity channel: it cannot distinguish decoding from guessing or reasoning from elimination, so it cannot constrain how success is achieved.
Differentiation often failed because it mistook variation in performance for variation in strategy, multiplying tasks without increasing the teacher's ability to see how they were solved.
Most adaptive learning platforms regulate the wrong variable, adjusting difficulty while a shortcut like process of elimination carries a learner through every level and gets reported as mastery.
The core design question is 'how else could a learner succeed here without doing the intended thinking?', and good tasks make the target cognitive operation the only reliable path to the answer.
Because learner ingenuity always outruns designer foresight, requisite variety is an asymptote to be approached through repeated observation, diagnosis and closing of shortcut paths.
quotes: This condition applies wherever one system attempts to shape the behaviour of another. Teaching and instructional design, at its core, is an attempt to stabilise particular cognitive outcomes in the face of learner variation. It is in essence, a regulatory enterprise.

In other words, if learners have more ways to succeed than your system has ways to detect and block easy shortcuts, the shortcuts will win. Not because learners are lazy or devious, but because they are rational agents navigating a system that has left paths of least resistance wide open.

In practice, it often failed because it mistook variation in performance for variation in strategy. It multiplied tasks without increasing the system’s capacity to detect how those tasks were being solved.

When multiple cognitive strategies can produce the same correct answer, binary scoring becomes blind. Recognition can masquerade as recall. Elimination can masquerade as understanding. Pattern familiarity can masquerade as reasoning.

This is the central disappointment of much educational technology: not that it lacks sophistication, but that its sophistication is deployed in the wrong direction. Engagement metrics, gamification, personalised difficulty curves, these are genuine technical achievements.

It begins with a question that many educators do not ask systematically: how else could a learner succeed here without doing the intended thinking? Every task has alternative solution paths, and those paths will be found.

This is not a counsel of despair about teachers, or technology, or learners. It is a precise description of what instructional design must accomplish and why it so often falls short. The problem is not effort or intention; it is regulatory variety.
